Allen Carr's book is very much a manual to condition yourself out of smoking but it's correctly named 'easyway' because frankly what's easier than just going from smoking to simply not doing it?

Edit: I had tried vaping etc. as well, all to no avail ultimately, though the e-cigs were definitely ok.

My father (who actually gave me the book) read the book and he's been off the smokes for about 10.

There's definitely a heavy personal component but tackling the thinking underpinning the habit apparently works. Some people reckon they never get a craving again. I've had a few situations happen where I felt the tickle, but it was more an opportunity to choose not to bother with it again.

I think breaking the habit down from a monolith to just a decision you keep making each time, and seeing failing as simply a setback for when you try again next week (or whenever), really brings it into perspective for what it is: just something you've chosen to do x times a day for the last x years and can quite easily not choose to do x times for the next x years.

One interesting thing is that for my old man realising he just liked the ritual of rolling cigarettes and could focus on something else really helped, but for me realising I was being compelled to interrupt my work doing a task I could never complete (there's no completion of smoking lol) really broke its back. It's weird what can trip the switch for you.

Best of luck to you however you choose to go about it. I hope you find the means to make it a breeze and enjoy your body recovering (that one's nice too).

I stopped vaping and didn't go back to smoking except when I drink (which is very rarely) but I still wanted to smoke/use nicotine sometimes. I eventually looked into Swedish snus. It's like chewing tobacco but it comes in a little pouch and you put it in your upper lip instead of the lower lip so it doesn't get so saturated with saliva and you don't need to spit. If you look into it snusing is not associated with oral cancer or other mouth/throat diseases, in fact studies of swedish men who use snus show that they have lower incidence of oral cancer than non-users. In Sweden (which has a massive nanny state government btw) they've even taken all the cancer warnings off the product in response to research. I really like snus and I only do it occasionally, if I drink usually, or just if I feel like it, and I've found it to satisfy my nicotine urge at those times, without any negative side effects. Snus also doesn't have the addictive aspect of the habit of bringing the ciggarette up to your mouth and doing the whole routine of smoking. I've found it to be basically not addictive at all, but to satisfy what I want when I feel like using nicotine (probably once or twice a week at this point).

Don't know how effective snus would be for helping you quit, but I would guess it's at least as helpful as nicotine patches and probably many times cheaper. Cigarette smoke has tons of chemicals besides nicotine that effect the feeling you get, and neither snus nor nicotine patches will deliver those chemicals (I've even found that different brands don't offer the same feelings, e.g., if you smoke Camels and then try an American Spirit, the AS isn't satisfying at all). But snus will deliver the nicotine at least and maybe help to prevent some of the withdrawal symptoms associated only with the nicotine itself. I quit smoking without using products but I use snus now more as a better way of getting nicotine when I feel like it.

If you decide to try snus be sure to get a brand that's actually made in Sweden as their process is highly regulated where as American brands (I think Camel might be the only one right now) are just some chemical saturated product they're calling "snus". I smoked for 10 years and quit smoking by vaping. I tried cold turkey, gum, patches, everything short of chantix (afraid of the side effects). Nothing worked for me. With vaping, I was able to slowly step down my nicotine level until I just stopped. The way I described it to people was that when I smoked, I needed a cigarette every 2 hours. With vaping, the craving is still there, but it feels more like, "it would be nice if I had a quick vape", but if I wasn't in a situation where that was possible, I had no problems waiting. I stepped down my nicotine level from 18mg/ml to 3 mg/ml over 2 years, and quit nicotine and vaping completely a little over 2 months ago. GreatDrok is correct in saying that there are 2 factors to quitting smoking, but where we disagree is that vaping helped me with both. Nicotine is a very addictive chemical, and by reducing the amount you're getting gradually, you can slowly wean yourself off. It took me about 2 years, and I was in no hurry, but at no time did I even think about smoking a cigarette, because I was still getting some nicotine. Secondly, the activity of smoking is replaced by the activity of vaping, which still emulates the desired or expected results of smoking; the act of inhaling something, filling your lungs with vapor, exhaling and seeing the cloud (please don't be a cloudsbroclouds guy though). With each step of reduction in nicotine, I also found myself reducing the time I had my vape with me. After a drop in nic level, I'd want to hit it a lot, then my use would normalize, then I would find myself leaving my vape at home for hours at a time. Once I could go an entire day at school or work without an issue, I'd drop to the next level of nicotine. It is a lengthy process, but it worked for me where nothing else had, so I am a firm believer. Good luck to you in whatever method you choose!
